We will now break this down using the **before–during–after** framework.

### 🔹 BEFORE: The Political Landscape, Party Positions, and Constitutional Expectations (Pre-1971)

#### 1. **Political Landscape**
- Pakistan was a federation of four provinces: **West Pakistan (Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, NWFP)** and **East Pakistan (Bangladesh)**.
- The **Awami League (AL)**, led by **Sheikh Mujibur Rahman**, had won a massive majority in the 1970 general elections — securing **160 out of 167 seats** in the National Assembly.
- The **Pakistan People’s Party (PPP)**, led by **Zulfikar Ali Bhutto**, won a strong mandate in **Punjab and Sindh**, but failed in East Pakistan.
- The **one-unit system** (which merged all provinces into a single administrative unit) was widely criticized as unjust and unrepresentative, especially in East Pakistan.

#### 2. **Party Positions**
- **Awami League (AL)**:
  - Advocated for **Six Points** — a federal structure with provincial autonomy, including:
    - Separate provincial governments
    - Control over taxation and revenue
    - Right to have their own defense and foreign policy
    - Separate judiciary
    - Right to manage natural resources
    - Right to have their own currency
  - Believed that only through these points could a truly democratic and equitable federation be built.
- **PPP (Bhutto)**:
  - Opposed the Six Points, fearing they would lead to **federal fragmentation** and weaken national unity.
  - Argued that the Six Points were part of an **Indian plot** to break up Pakistan.
  - Wanted a **strong central government** with federal control over key areas like defense and foreign policy.
- **Military Government (Yahya Khan)**:
  - Initially supported the idea of a national assembly and elections.
  - But increasingly resisted the Six Points, fearing loss of central control.
  - Believed that a strong central government was necessary to maintain stability.

#### 3. **Constitutional Expectations**
- The **Legal Framework Order (LFO) of 1970** laid out the structure of the proposed constitution:
  - National Assembly would be elected.
  - The President (Yahya Khan) would decide when the National Assembly would convene.
  - The constitution would be drafted by a joint committee of political parties and the military.
- There was **expectation of a democratic, federal constitution** that would reflect the will of the people — especially in East Pakistan.
- The **1956 and 1962 constitutions** were seen as outdated, centralized, and unrepresentative of provincial demands.

> ✅ **Key Takeaway (Before):**  
> The 1971 period was marked by a **deep constitutional crisis** — a clash between democratic aspirations (especially from East Pakistan) and centralized, military-led governance. The 1970 elections had created a democratic mandate, but the refusal to accept the Six Points and the postponement of the National Assembly session shattered trust in the federal government.

---

### 🔹 DURING: The Crisis, Conflict, and Constitutional Breakdown (1970–1971)

#### 1. **Election Results (December 1970)**
- Awami League won a clear majority in East Pakistan.
- PPP won in West Pakistan.
- The National Assembly was expected to meet in Dhaka on **March 3, 1971**.

#### 2. **The Six-Point Crisis**
- On **February 15**, Bhutto announced that the PPP would **not attend** the National Assembly unless there was **reciprocity** (i.e., concessions from the AL).
- On **February 21**, Sheikh Mujib declared:  
  > “Our stand is absolutely clear. The constitution will be framed on the basis of the six points.”
- This led to a **deadlock** between the two major parties.

#### 3. **Postponement of the National Assembly (March 25, 1971)**
- Under pressure from the PPP, President Yahya Khan **postponed** the session.
- This was seen as a **betrayal

## 🔁 Timeline of Key Amendments: Before & After

---

### 📌 1. **Eighth Amendment (1985)**  
> *“Changed the government from a parliamentary system to a semi-presidential system.”*

| Aspect | Before (1973 Constitution) | After (1985 – 8th Amendment) |
|-------|----------------------------|------------------------------|
| **System Type** | Parliamentary Republic | Semi-Presidential System |
| **Presidential Power** | Limited; President had ceremonial role | Expanded: President gained significant powers |
| **Military Appointments** | Prime Minister controlled military appointments | President gained authority to appoint and dismiss military leaders |
| **Judicial Independence** | Supreme Court had full independence | Not directly affected, but power imbalance created tension |
| **Prime Minister Power** | Prime Minister was head of government; could dismiss PM | Prime Minister weakened; President could override decisions |
| **Impact** | Clear separation of powers | Centralization of power in the executive; President became more powerful |

> ✅ **Key Shift**: From parliamentary to semi-presidential → President gains control over military and can override PM.

---

### 📌 2. **Seventeenth Amendment (2004)**  
> *“Reversed the 1985 expansion of presidential powers.”*

| Aspect | Before (Post-1985) | After (2004 – 17th Amendment) |
|-------|--------------------|-------------------------------|
| **System Type** | Semi-presidential (post-1985) | Back to parliamentary system |
| **Military Appointments** | President controlled appointments | Prime Minister regained control |
| **Presidential Powers** | Expanded (e.g., dissolve parliament, appoint judges) | Reduced significantly |
| **Prime Minister Power** | Weakened | Strengthened; now head of government with real authority |
| **Judicial Independence** | Slightly threatened | Improved due to reduced executive interference |
| **Impact** | Power shift toward President | Restoration of democratic balance; PM gains legitimacy |

> ✅ **Key Shift**: Reversal of 1985 → Return to parliamentary system; PM regains authority.

> ⚠️ *Note: This was a temporary reversal — the 18th Amendment later re-established the parliamentary system permanently.*

---

### 📌 3. **Eighteenth Amendment (2010)**  
> *“Largest change: Reversed presidential expansions, returned to parliamentary republic.”*

| Aspect | Before (2010) | After (2010 – 18th Amendment) |
|-------|---------------|-------------------------------|
| **System Type** | Semi-presidential (after 1985 & 2004) | Fully **Parliamentary Republic** |
| **Presidential Powers** | Broad (military, judiciary, dissolution) | Severely limited; ceremonial role only |
| **Prime Minister Power** | Weak | **Restored full authority** over government, budget, and judiciary |
| **Judicial Independence** | Under threat | **Fully secured**; no executive interference |
| **Judicial Appointment** | President could appoint judges | Prime Minister now appoints judges (with Senate approval) |
| **Constitutional Safeguards** | No clear treason clause | Introduced **high treason** for any attempt to subvert or suspend the Constitution |
| **Impact** | Executive overreach | Democratic restoration; strengthened checks and balances |

> ✅ **Key Shift**: Permanent return to parliamentary democracy; PM becomes dominant figure.

> 🏁 **This is the most significant change** — it redefined Pakistan’s governance model and restored democratic norms.
